conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or lecture. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. Your answers stay confidential, and any score we get is just a starting point for conversation and support, not a label.

We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to begin?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve noticed it’s gotten a lot harder. I used to laugh easily, but lately even the little things that should be funny just feel… flat. A couple of times my partner tried to joke to lighten the mood, and I barely managed a smile. It’s like the joy is stuck somewhere.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, I can manage a little chuckle every now and then, but most of the time it feels forced. It’s like I have to remind myself to laugh, and even when I do, it doesn’t last or feel natural.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to, but it’s hard. I’ll think, “Maybe I’ll feel better if I go for coffee with a friend,” yet when the time comes it feels like such a chore that I usually stay home. Even little things—watching a show I used to like or taking the baby for a walk—don’t excite me the way they used to. I still do them, hoping they’ll lift my mood, but the enjoyment just isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes… a lot of the time. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not feeding him properly or I missed his sleepy cues. When he wouldn’t settle last night, I kept replaying everything I’d done, convinced I’d messed up his routine. Even little things, like dropping a burp cloth, make me feel like I’m failing at being a mom. I know it sounds silly, but the guilt just jumps on me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often, yeah. Sometimes my heart just starts racing and I can’t settle, even when nothing specific has happened. I’ll lie in bed running through every worst-case scenario—what if the baby stops breathing, what if I’m missing some illness, what if I’m doing everything wrong. There’s no real reason for it in that moment, but I can’t shake the dread. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes... it hits out of nowhere. I'll be folding laundry while the baby naps and suddenly feel this wave of fear, like something awful is about to happen. My chest gets tight, I can't catch my breath, and I have to sit down. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and watching the baby monitor like crazy. There's nothing actually wrong, but in those moments I'm convinced there is.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between feedings, laundry, trying to shower, answering texts I never get to—some mornings I open my eyes and feel like I’m already drowning. I make lists, but the minute the baby cries everything unravels. I keep telling myself millions of moms do this, so why can’t I cope? I manage to get the essentials done, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie there after the night feed, exhausted but my mind just won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong—did I burp him long enough, why was he so fussy, am I already failing him? The worries swirl around and before I know it an hour’s passed and I’m still wide awake, listening to every little sound from the crib. Even when I do drift off I jerk awake at the tiniest whimper. It’s like the sadness and anxiety just won’t let my body shut down.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, honestly. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t shake off. I wake up already feeling low, and it just lingers—while I feed him, while I change him, while I try to eat something myself. I’ll see pictures of smiling moms online and wonder why I can’t feel that way. There are moments when I’ll get distracted for a bit, but the sadness always creeps back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it comes in waves. A couple of nights ago the baby wouldn’t latch, and I just burst into tears—couldn’t stop. Sometimes it’s smaller things, like seeing a tiny outfit he’s already outgrown; I’ll feel ridiculous, but the tears just start flowing. It’s not every single day, but definitely a few times a week I end up crying in the nursery or while I’m rocking him, trying to stay quiet so no one hears me.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared that the joy and motivation you once had have been replaced by a persistent heaviness that colors nearly every part of your day. Laughing now feels forced, simple pleasures seem like chores, and waves of worry or even panic arrive without warning, leaving you breathless and shaky. You blame yourself for every hiccup in your baby's care, carry a constant sense of falling short, and cry more often than you'd like. Sleep brings little rest because your mind races with fears and replays of perceived mistakes. Despite these struggles you remain devoted to your baby and want desperately to feel better so you can be the mom you hope to be. **Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include Patient reports only occasional forced chuckles, indicating a clear reduction in ability to laugh, matching "Definitely not so much now", Patient describes persistent loss of anticipatory pleasure and motivation across activities that previously brought joy, matching "Hardly at all", Patient describes pervasive, daily self-blame for ordinary events, aligning with "most of the time", Patient reports frequent, intense, intrusive worries and physical anxiety symptoms "very often" without triggers, matching "Yes, very often", "Yes, quite a lot", She reports struggling "most days" and feeling overwhelmed, which aligns with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual" rather than the more severe "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all.", Patient describes nightly sleep disruption caused by persistent sadness and anxiety, with racing thoughts and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time", Patient reports sadness "most of the time," describing it as persistent and pervasive throughout daily activities, aligning with the highest severity option., Patient describes crying episodes several times per week triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often") **Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. Your answers meet core DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day (heavy blanket), diminished interest or pleasure (enjoyment just isn't really there), inappropriate guilt (failing as a mom), recurrent panic and anxiety, sleep disturbance unrelated to infant care, and functional impairment. Combined score of 24 mandates urgent follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice. **Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:** 1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your obstetrician, primary care provider, or perinatal mental health specialist within the next few days 2. Bring this EPDS result to your visit; discuss medication options including sertraline or escitalopram compatible with breastfeeding if desired 3. Ask about evidence-based therapy such as cognitive-behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy focused on postpartum issues 4. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or friends-to cover night feeds once nightly so you can obtain a 4-5 hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep 5. Practice brief self-care: 5-minute outdoor daylight walk, balanced meals, and hydration; set a phone reminder to eat every 4 hours 6. Use a simple grounding technique during panic: inhale 4 seconds, hold 4, exhale 6; repeat 5 cycles while naming 5 things you can see 7. Limit social media comparisons; consider muting accounts that trigger feelings of inadequacy 8. Keep emergency numbers handy: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 or Postpartum Support International text 800-944-4773 9. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after treatment begins Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms (self-report):
- Persistent low mood, “heavy blanket” most of the day, tearful episodes 3–4×/week  
- Marked anhedonia: forced laughter, no anticipation of enjoyment, activities feel “like a chore”  
- Excessive self-blame / inappropriate guilt regarding infant care; feels “failing as a mom”  
- Recurrent, intrusive “worst-case-scenario” worries; un-cued panic episodes with chest tightness & breathlessness occurring multiple times per week  
- Sleep disruption: difficulty returning to sleep after infant feeds, racing thoughts, hyper-arousal to baby sounds  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed; reports “already drowning” each morning, minimal coping reserve  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm (specifically endorsed “no” on Q10)

Pattern: symptoms present most days and interfere with functioning; onset since delivery.

Screening significance: high endorsement (≥ 8/10 items) consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features; meets threshold for further clinical evaluation.

Risk factors noted: prolonged sadness, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety/panic, sleep loss, impaired coping—no acute safety concerns per patient denial of self-harm.

Plan: Recommend comprehensive diagnostic assessment (DSM-5 criteria), psycho-education, and discussion of evidence-based treatment options; consider Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale for standardized score and monitoring.
